Embrapa, the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation, is Brazil's state run farm research agency, founded in 1973 under the Ministry of Agriculture and based in Brasília.

In the early 1970s Brazil imported much of its food. Its vast tropical savanna, the Cerrado, was thought useless for crops: the soil was acidic and poor. Embrapa set out to change that, with dozens of research centres across the country and scientists trained abroad.

  • Spreading lime and phosphorus made Cerrado soils fertile.
  • Researchers bred soybean varieties that grow in the tropics, where they had never done well.
  • Bacteria added to seeds let soybeans make their own nitrogen, saving fertiliser.
  • They promoted no till farming and mixed crop and cattle systems.

The results were huge. Within a few decades Brazil became one of the world's largest exporters of soybeans, beef, chicken, sugar and coffee. In 2006 the World Food Prize went to Brazilians who led this work. Like the Green Revolution in Asia, it showed how science can change a nation's farming.

The farm boom also had a cost: much of the Cerrado's native vegetation has been cleared.
sum: Embrapa, the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation, is Brazil's state run farm research agency, founded in 1973 under the Ministry of Agriculture and based in Brasília.
